title: Stomata
summary: Stomata are tiny pores (openings) on the surface of leaves and stems that plants use to breathe. They open to let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis and close to save water. Explore how guard cells control these gates.

compareCandidate.label: Stomata open vs. closed
compareCandidate.description: Open stomata let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, but also let water escape. Closed stomata save water but keep carbon dioxide out. The plant balances these by opening when there is light and closing when it is dry.

processes: Gas exchange - carbon dioxide in, oxygen out
Opening and closing by guard cells
plainLanguageExplanation: A stoma (plural stomata) is a tiny pore, or opening, on the surface of a leaf. Each stoma is controlled by two guard cells that swell up and bend to open it, or relax to close it. While open, the leaf can take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and let out the oxygen it makes. But opening also lets water escape as steam. So plants open their stomata mainly when there is light to photosynthesize in the daytime, and close them at night or when they must save water - like on a hot, dry day.

whyItMatters: Stomata are the plant's gates for the two most important gases for life: carbon dioxide it needs to make food, and oxygen it gives as a byproduct. They also control how much water a plant loses, so they're a plant's balance key for breathing and conserving water.
tagline: The plant's tiny adjustable air gates
didYouKnow: A single small leaf can have millions of stomata, each one a tiny door controlled by two cells.
